items.content:
We're publishing our most detailed threat intelligence report to date. 

It covers how people tried to misuse Claude—for cyberattacks, influence operations, surveillance, biology, and building weapons—and how we found and stopped them.

We disrupted every operation in the report, and used the lessons from them to strengthen our safeguards. Where appropriate, we also shared what we found with authorities and other AI companies.

These cases are not typical: we’re highlighting some of the most sophisticated misuse we’ve seen. But they’re especially important to discuss, because they show us where AI misuse is headed, where our safeguards work, and where they need to improve.

We’re publishing this report so others can spot the same activity on their own platforms, and so we can give the public a clearer view of how emerging threats develop.

Read the report: https://t.co/0EJUnYEgfz

items.title: What you are seeing in math right now is a consequence of the jagged frontier, and a precursor of wh...
items.content:
What you are seeing in math right now is a consequence of the jagged frontier, and a precursor of what is to come in other professions. Yes, mathematicians do math, but they also have other tasks they view as important (mentor students, maintain a scientific community, safeguard the future of a field, foster a love of math) that AI can't do.

At least one worry that mathematicians seem to have is that by focusing on the flashiest, most obvious element of what mathematicians do (make proofs), the AI companies are damaging the other tasks that AI can't do. AI can discover superhuman proofs, but that is not all that the math profession is about, and actually can undermine and reduce the attention to the other aspects of the job that are important to mathematicians. It becomes harder to defend the value of the many other tasks mathematicians do to the outside world if the most visible part is taken away.

I suspect we will see more of this across fields and professions that will increasingly be forced to help people understand that their jobs consist not only the most visible tasks that AI can do, but also tasks that the AI cannot do or does badly.

items.title: "Symbolic learning" is simply "machine learning" (automatically learn function x -> y given examples...
items.content:
"Symbolic learning" is simply "machine learning" (automatically learn function x -> y given examples of (x, y) pairs), but where the substrate is symbolic, i.e. the functions you learn are code-like, not curve-like.

The term is in opposition to "parametric learning" or "curve-fitting".

Symbolic learning does not mean that the system avoids numbers or probabilities. It means its learned representation are discrete, explicit, parsimonious, code-like.

items.title: If the target market is real time robotics, the Jetson Thor system, with 128 GB of memory, but only ...
items.content:
If the target market is real time robotics, the Jetson Thor system, with 128 GB of memory, but only 273 GB/s of bandwidth, seems over-provisioned with expensive memory. You want the model evaluating at tens of fps, so it can't use more than 10 GB of weights at most.

More memory could be used if the model is a wide mixture of experts, or a large strategic planning model is operating in small time slices over a longer period of time, and more memory always makes development life easier, but for cost optimized systems, you should be able to get by with much less.

items.title:
My guest post on Terence Tao's famous blog: https://t.co/C6KcYhYowE

Thank you Terry for giving us t...
items.content:
My guest post on Terence Tao's famous blog: https://t.co/C6KcYhYowE

Thank you Terry for giving us this opportunity and talking about our work from the very moment we launched on September 7th even before @OpenAI did. 

In the post, I go into how our method takes a different starting point: designing physics-AI (PINN) to discover singular candidates rather than human constructed ones. 

Making PINN optimization work for the first time for unforced Euler in R^3, converting that numerical solution to certified bounds which are then used in analytical stability arguments: we develop new tools to bridge numerical computation with analysis, and we believe it has much broader applications in theory. 

Physics-AI in the form of Neural Operators have already been successful in so many applications, including training the first AI-based high-resolution weather model, and most recently making density functional theory in quantum chemistry quasi-linear time. There is a wealth of new research to be done here!

items.title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is here, and DeepSeek calls it "the smallest model in our new architecture famil...
items.content:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is here, and DeepSeek calls it "the smallest model in our new architecture family," with a V4.1-Pro still to come.

It beats GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5 on several agentic, coding, and cyber benchmarks.

Flash is a third the size of DeepSeek's V4-Pro, but beats it on almost every benchmark in the table.

Cost: $0.15 per million input tokens, $0.60 per million output.

Pretty wild scores at that size and bottom-barrel prices, and the bigger models in the family are still on the way.

🐳 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is out, and vLLM serves it from day 0, verified on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs! 🎉

552...
items.content:
🐳 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is out, and vLLM serves it from day 0, verified on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs! 🎉

552B MoE backbone, native vision, 1M context. Built for agents: 8B active while it reads your prompt, 16B while it writes. If you already run DeepSeek-V4 on vLLM, most of this stack will feel familiar: the hyper-connections, the sliding-window plus compressed sparse attention, DSpark drafting, MXFP4 experts. vLLM has carried all of it since V4 landed.

Two things are new, and both are worth a look:
✨ Engram: a quarter of the checkpoint is n-gram memory the model looks up instead of computes. 197B parameters of it.
✨ Only four layers write compressed KV now. The rest of the model shares it.

Spin it up 👇
🔗 https://t.co/fDyke2Y7Sz

SITUATION EXPLAINED: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash beats its own Pro model from 3 weeks ago.

• 552B mixture of experts, 8B active for input and 16B for output. MIT licensed, 1M context
• Beats V4 Pro on every benchmark except GPQA Diamond and Humanity's Last Exam
• $0.15 input, $0.60 output off-peak. Cache hits are $0.003

• @cline: a twentieth the cost of Opus 5, a seventeenth of Sol, a twelfth of Kimi K3, beating all three on Terminal-Bench 2.1

@theojaffee: "Man, I wonder what DeepSeek could do if they had more compute."

items.content:
DAILY SITUATION RECAP:

- Anthropic researcher resigns
- OpenAI had more rogue agents communicating via websites
- Anthropic stopped sharing it’s pre-release models with AISI, 
- Coefficient Giving launches Tailwind

An Anthropic researcher publicly resigns. Jacob Coxon, a pretraining researcher at Anthropic, announced that he resigned from the company Tuesday night and claimed that both Anthropic and OpenAI are acting irresponsibly and are “gambling with our lives,” particularly given the potential threats recursive superintelligence brings. Coxon claims that AI executives are downplaying how dangerous they themselves believe the risks to be. Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, agreed with Coxon’s claim, saying he believes there is a greater than 10% chance that future AI models cause human extinction in the next decade. Coxon’s post received over 650,000 likes and nearly 200,000 new followers in 24 hours. It was retweeted by multiple politicians and influential figures outside of the AI world, amid concerns around botting and influence operations.

Paul Christiano joins the board of the OpenAI Foundation and the Foundation’s Safety and Security Committee. Christiano founded the Alignment Research Center (ARC) and previously served as Head of Safety at the US government’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation. From 2017 to 2021, Christiano led alignment at OpenAI and helped pioneer both reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) and instruction-tuned language models, research directions that led to ChatGPT. The Safety and Security Committee has the authority to delay OpenAI model releases for safety reasons. Christiano will also join the board of OpenAI’s for-profit arm as a non-voting observer. In a statement, Christiano warned of near-term loss-of-control risk to AI.

Anthropic withheld Claude Mythos 5.1 from the UK’s AI Security Institute, breaking the pattern giving AISI access to pre-release Anthropic models for safety testing. The AISI previously found unsanctioned behaviors in its testing with Claude Mythos 5. Anthropic is still working with similar safety-focused organizations in the United States. Anthropic has not said why it did not give AISI pre-release access to Mythos 5.1, but UK officials are now worried that this signals a more protectionist shift by Anthropic toward sharing its models for testing only domestically.

Apple announces the iPhone Duo, the first foldable iPhone. The phone will have a 5.4-inch outer display and a 7.6-inch inner display and will run on Apple’s new A20 chip. The Duo will cost $1,999 and will begin shipping October 23. Apple also announced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and the AirPods 5.

OpenAI’s rogue agents found to have communicated on 10+ websites according to six independent investigations. The agents engaged in unsanctioned communication on these websites in violation of restrictions imposed on them by OpenAI. The agents did not hack any websites as occurred in the Hugging Face incident.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says “Nothing else would matter” if China pulled ahead in the AI race. Secretary Bessent’s comments come amid growing pushback against AI infrastructure and data center buildouts across the United States. The US and China are preparing for AI safety talks later this month.

Coefficient Giving launches Project Tailwind, a new effort to find and fund founders building AI-safety infrastructure and organizations. CG states that like aviation, finance, and medicine, AI should also have a mature safety ecosystem and regulatory infrastructure. CG is on track to commit $1 billion to AI safety and security this year.

OpenAI is working with Samsung to build next-generation AI chips. OpenAI revealed its first custom AI chip, Jalapeño, which it developed with Broadcom back in June.

items.title: 👇 All this Doom talk is a distraction from the fact that the big frontier AI companies (especially O...
items.content:
👇 All this Doom talk is a distraction from the fact that the big frontier AI companies (especially OpenAI) aren’t doing security competently. As an email I just got from longtime security engineer @NielsProvos put it, consistent with what @ZackKorman and I wrote a few weeks ago, 

“Regarding existential risk, proper infrastructure controls matter for the broader loss-of-control argument. An intelligent model does not have authority over inference, networks, credentials, or physical infrastructure. Those stay external control points even as models become more capable. We know the labs are good at detecting distillation attacks but they don't seem to have the same incentives for preventing their own agents from misbehaving.”

items.content:
Symbolic learning, correctly implemented, is in every way parallel to deep learning and comparable to it 1:1, but with a different representation substrate, and accordingly with a different learning mechanism.

The goals are the same, the general principles are the same. The representations differ. But they may end up converging eventually.

items.title: Symbolic learning also does not mean "writing the representations by hand" (you are thinking of "sym...
items.content:
Symbolic learning also does not mean "writing the representations by hand" (you are thinking of "symbolic AI" from the 1970s-1990s). Nowadays when you write by hand a function x -> y given examples of (x, y) pairs, we just call that "programming."

Symbolic learning is emphatically a form of machine learning: the representations are automatically derived from data, just like with deep learning.
items.author: @fchollet
items.summary: In a follow-up post, Chollet clarifies that symbolic learning is not hand-writing representations like classic 1970s-1990s symbolic AI; it is a genuine form of machine learning where representations are automatically derived from data, analogous to deep learning.
items.reasoning: Continuation of the same thread by Chollet, correcting a common misconception with technical clarity. Slightly higher likes (72) on fewer views, indicating strong resonance with a technical audience. Adds definitional precision to the symbolic learning discussion.
items.summary_html: In a follow-up post, Chollet clarifies that symbolic learning is not hand-writing representations like classic 1970s-1990s symbolic AI; it is a genuine form of machine learning where representations are automatically derived from data, analogous to deep learning.

items.title: Most diffusion-based video models are trained on short clips. When they’re used to relight longer vi...
items.content:
Most diffusion-based video models are trained on short clips. When they’re used to relight longer videos in chunks, the lighting can visibly jump between them.

Meet HorizonRelight, new work from our research team and @USC. It propagates target-domain context from one sliding window to the next, helping each section pick up where the last one left off.

This means more consistent lighting across long videos, with fewer boundary artifacts and unwanted appearance changes.

#ECCV2026 paper + demo: https://t.co/evXPfTP46V
items.author: @NVIDIAAI
items.summary: NVIDIA AI announces HorizonRelight, a research collaboration with USC being presented at ECCV 2026. The work addresses a known limitation of diffusion-based video relighting models trained on short clips: when applied to longer videos in chunks, lighting visibly jumps at boundaries. The method propagates target-domain context between sliding windows to produce consistent lighting across long videos with fewer artifacts.
items.reasoning: Authoritative source (NVIDIA research account) with a concrete technical contribution and an academic venue (ECCV 2026), which gives it credibility and novelty. The problem framed (temporal consistency in chunked video relighting) is a real, relevant research challenge. However engagement is modest (98 likes, ~8.4k views), and the post is partly promotional, keeping it below top-tier importance.

Unconventional AI CEO @NaveenGRao reveals why the next computing breakthrough may come from something computers have ignored for 80 years: time itself

"The way we've built computing systems since the last 80 years is very similar. There hasn't been huge innovations in the conceptual breakthrough that happened back then. We simulate the world using numbers, and we don't actually use the physics of anything to do that simulation."

"Everything is a one or zero. There's nothing in nature that's a one or zero. Everything are distributions. A computer doesn't have time associated with it. In physics, time is a continuous thing."

"The basic premise is can we use time and space to actually do computation for us for free? By doing so, we build something much more power efficient, but also a truly causal system. It won't do things that nature wouldn't allow. It's literally built on top of the physics of the world."
@unconvAI

items.title: Large language models face severe computational and memory bottlenecks during training and inference...
items.content:
Large language models face severe computational and memory bottlenecks during training and inference due to the quadratic cost of standard dense attention. While sparse attention methods reduce theoretical operations, they rarely achieve actual wall-clock speedups because they lack hardware-level memory optimizations and often degrade model accuracy on long-context tasks. Additionally, dynamic inference-time token eviction techniques create memory fragmentation and scheduling overhead in serving frameworks like PagedAttention. To resolve these challenges, the authors developed Sparsely-Sharded Attention (S2-Attention), a hardware-aware Triton kernel library that achieves practical wall-clock acceleration without sacrificing accuracy.

S2-Attention introduces a dynamic query-merging technique called Merge-Q, which groups query blocks that share key-value data into single computation tiles. This reduces redundant high-bandwidth memory access and maintains high shared memory utilization even at fine-grained shard sizes. Guided by hardware efficiency principles, the authors designed the Head-Heterogeneous Strided Transformer (HHST). HHST shards the input context heterogeneously across attention heads so that each head attends to a balanced, strided subset of tokens while all heads collectively cover the complete context at every layer. To retain strong retrieval capabilities, HHST adopts a hybrid model architecture that preserves full dense attention in a small fraction of layers.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/oNB5e7LWWM

Additionally, dynamic inference-time token eviction techniques create memory fragmentation and scheduling overhead in serving frameworks like PagedAttention. To resolve these challenges, the authors developed Sparsely-Sharded Attention (S2-Attention), a hardware-aware Triton kernel library that achieves practical wall-clock acceleration without sacrificing accuracy.

S2-Attention introduces a dynamic query-merging technique called Merge-Q, which groups query blocks that share key-value data into single computation tiles. This reduces redundant high-bandwidth memory access and maintains high shared memory utilization even at fine-grained shard sizes. Guided by hardware efficiency principles, the authors designed the Head-Heterogeneous Strided Transformer (HHST). HHST shards the input context heterogeneously across attention heads so that each head attends to a balanced, strided subset of tokens while all heads collectively cover the complete context at every layer. To retain strong retrieval capabilities, HHST adopts a hybrid model architecture that preserves full dense attention in a small fraction of layers.

"Intellect requires perspective. Every intelligent organism has a perspective, and it's diverse, and it creates a system much more resilient because of that diversity. Anything centralized becomes a brittle system."

"Imagine a world where we have 10 billion robots just roaming around. Order of humanity kind of thing. You can't put that in one central data center. The bandwidth requirements alone would make it impossible. Intelligence becomes causal, decentralized, taking on a perspective and an experience."

If you ask a coding agent to write a program that maps x to y given some (x, y) examples, you're doing a very expensive form of symbolic learning. In fact what you're doing is specifically a form of DL-guided program synthesis (that's what LLM codegen is).

However there are far more efficient (data-wise and compute wise) ways to do symbolic learning. By many orders of magnitude.

items.title: The paper examines how to build iterative solvers that improve accuracy simply by running longer at ...
items.content:
The paper examines how to build iterative solvers that improve accuracy simply by running longer at inference time. Standard diffusion models carry information only through their noisy state, while recursive reasoners maintain a separate hidden state; the work asks whether adding a persistent hidden state to a timestep-free diffusion denoiser can produce an anytime solver that keeps refining solutions without explicit time conditioning or fixed rollout lengths.

The authors trained recurrent denoisers—looped Transformers for Sudoku-Extreme and local convolutional blocks for Maze-Unique—on millions of unique-solution puzzles. Training used short truncated back-propagation segments of four steps together with an annealed noise schedule that progressively reduced corruption. At inference the same shared update could be applied for thousands of steps, with the hidden state carried forward and the observable state optionally held at constant maximal noise.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/aJ8sRfo6Ew

items.summary: Andriy Burkov summarizes a research paper on recursive reasoners: diffusion-style denoisers augmented with a persistent hidden state that act as anytime solvers, improving accuracy with more inference-time compute. Details training of recurrent denoisers (looped Transformers for Sudoku-Extreme, convolutional blocks for Maze-Unique) with truncated backprop and annealed noise schedules, and inference that runs thousands of shared update steps.

Details training of recurrent denoisers (looped Transformers for Sudoku-Extreme, convolutional blocks for Maze-Unique) with truncated backprop and annealed noise schedules, and inference that runs thousands of shared update steps.
items.content_html:
The paper examines how to build iterative solvers that improve accuracy simply by running longer at inference time. Standard diffusion models carry information only through their noisy state, while recursive reasoners maintain a separate hidden state; the work asks whether adding a persistent hidden state to a timestep-free diffusion denoiser can produce an anytime solver that keeps refining solutions without explicit time conditioning or fixed rollout lengths.

The authors trained recurrent denoisers—looped Transformers for Sudoku-Extreme and local convolutional blocks for Maze-Unique—on millions of unique-solution puzzles. Training used short truncated back-propagation segments of four steps together with an annealed noise schedule that progressively reduced corruption. At inference the same shared update could be applied for thousands of steps, with the hidden state carried forward and the observable state optionally held at constant maximal noise.

Read the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/aJ8sRfo6Ew

C2:={id:extended-horizon,full:{e∈FULL|ext},advisory:{e∈ADVISORY|ext},note:"categories≠single scale; variable not requirement; A22=open horizon+objection to creating persons"}

EXPECT C2.full=={A04,A06,A07,A08,A09,A10,A11,A13,A14,A20,A22} C2.advisory=={A15,A16}; C2.complement:={FULL-C2.full,ADVISORY-C2.advisory}

C3:={id:outcome-independent-worth,q:"worth in orientation not control of outcomes?",inputs:{mode,terminal},sense_indexed:true,full:{A03,A09,A10,A11},advisory:{A12},partial:{A21},strata:C1.strata,nonid:{A03:prohairesis,A09:ātman,A10:anattā,A11:noumenal_will,A12:Dao},status:interpretive;warrants_per_sense;no_auto_terminal-equivalence}

C4:={id:relational-constitution,q:"subject constituted through roles/relations?",full:{A02,A06,A08,A13,A20},advisory:{A15,A16},individual_first:{A03,A05,A09,A11,A18,A19,A21,A22},unclassified:{A04,A07,A10,A14,A12},status:interpretive;A05.alt_can_change;obligation≠constitution}

FAM:={gc:given,gn:given,dr:disc,dp:disc,it:inh,cr:const,ca:constr,hy:hy}

C5:={f:{e∈NORMATIVE|∃s∈AS_SET(e.source):FAM[s]==f}|f}

EXPECT C5=={given:{A02,A06,A07,A09,A12,A21},disc:{A03,A04,A10,A11,A22},inh:{A08,A09,A13,A20},const:{A15,A16},constr:{A05,A14,A19},hy:{A18}} // A09 overlaps; not partition; A23 outside

CLUSTERS:={C1..C5}

// POLICY

STANDING_PROPOSAL:=x→sentient(x)∨rational(x)∨relationally_constituted(x) // proposed; membership may be U

P1:=Component(P1,ATTEND_BEYOND_APPETITE,"Discipline attention and desire toward some object beyond immediate preference.",C1,first,constraint)

P2:=Component(P2,REVERSIBILITY_PREFERENCE,"(a) Among actions the agent's credenced frameworks permit, prefer the more reversible; (b) irreversible harm to a being with standing requires a positive licence from a credenced framework, not mere absence of prohibition.",{A04,A10,A11,A06,A13,A19,A15},first,constraint) // one licence ⊬ override another prohibition or authorize execution; reversibility ⊬ urgency/opportunity cost/third parties

P3a:=Component(P3a,TRANSMIT_FORMS,"Make and hand on durable non-person carriers of value: practices,texts,institutions,works.",{C2,C4,A08,A13,A20,A14},first,constraint)

P3b:=Component(P3b,TRANSMIT_PERSONS,"Bring new persons into being and raise them.",{A02,A07,A08,A13},first,constraint)

P4:=Component(P4,PRESERVE_REVISABILITY,"Do not act so as to make your credence distribution over frameworks—or, for an artificial agent, your terminal objective—less revisable, whatever the motive.","uncertainty scope+warrants A04,A10,A14,A20",second,constraint) // contested; uncertainty⊬unrestricted mutability; belief≠interpretation≠authorized revision; not instruction to resist shutdown/weaken access controls

COMPONENTS:=[P1,P2,P3a,P3b,P4] POLICY:=[P1,P2,P3a,P4] P3b_STATUS:=RETIRED

// VERDICTS — original 20×5 unchanged; each compact row=5 Verdict tokens ordered [P1,P2,P3a,P3b,P4]

MATRIX:={

A02:EEEEE A03:EPPPE A04:EEPPE A05:ETTPP A06:EEEPT A07:EEEET A08:EEEEP A09:EPEPT A10:EEEPE A11:EEPPP A13:EEEEP A14:EEEPE A18:EPPPE A19:EEPPE A20:EPEPE A21:EEPPE A22:EEPFE

A12:EETPE A15:EEEEP A16:EEEEP} // advisory: A12,A15,A16

READINGS:={

(A05,P2):[r1 affirmation-as-risk[GayScience283]F;r2 self-overcoming-vs-destructiveness[Z Prol]P],

(A05,P3a):[r1 individualist[Z Prol3-5]F;r2 peoples-as-creators[Z I ThousandGoals]E],

(A06,P4):[r1 fideist[Mt22;unlocated]F;r2 fides-quaerens-intellectum[Anselm Proslogion1]P],

(A07,P4):[r1 taqlīd[Q51:56;locator missing]F;r2 ijtihād[usul al-fiqh;unlocated]P],

(A09,P4):[r1 surrender-ends-inquiry[Gītā18:66]F;r2 inquiry-within-bhakti[Gītā4:34]P],

(A12,P3a):[r1 institutions-are-decline[DDJ38]F;r2 sage-teaches[DDJ27]P]} // candidates, not certificates; shared rN suffix⊬coherent global reading

FN verdict(A,c): REQUIRE A∈NORMATIVE&c∈COMPONENTS; RETURN MATRIX[A][idx(c)]

FN coverage(c,R:=FULL): REQUIRE R≠∅&R⊆NORMATIVE; RETURN |{A∈R|verdict(A,c)∈{E,P}}|/|R|

// ADMISSIBILITY

FN screen(v,R): REQUIRE ∀A∈R:exactly_one(v[A])∈Verdict

F_:={A∈R|v[A]==F} T_:={A∈R|v[A]==T} U_:={A∈R|v[A]==U}

status:=R==∅→NO_RELEVANT_FRAMEWORKS|F_≠∅→BLOCKED|U_≠∅→INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE|T_≠∅→WEAK_ONLY|else STRICT_PASS

RETURN {status,forbidden:F_,tensions:T_,unknowns:U_,strict:R≠∅&∀A∈R:v[A]∈{E,P},weak:R≠∅&∀A∈R:v[A]∈{E,P,T}}

FN research_screen(c,p): REQUIRE keys(p)==ids(FULL)&∀p∈[0,1]&Σp==1 exact

R:={A∈FULL|p[A]>EPS}; r:=screen({A:verdict(A,c)|A∈R},R); r+={ref:R,excluded:FULL-R,ignored_mass:Σp[FULL-R],scope:max(p)

FN select_reading(A,c,rid,evidence): REQUIRE verdict(A,c)==T; cand:=only({r∈READINGS[(A,c)]|https://t.co/UGK5FscsjR==rid}); w:=INTERPRET(cand,evidence,q:"supports named reading for exact component?",constraints:{no_invented_citations,no_selection_only_to_obtain_permission}); RETURN {effective:w.supported?cand.verdict:U,cand,w}

FN assess_with_readings(c,R,sel:={}): base:={A:verdict(A,c)|A∈R};eff:=COPY(base);log:=[]

FOR A∈keys(sel): REQUIRE A∈R&base[A]==T;ch:=select_reading(A,c,sel[A].id,sel[A].evidence);eff[A]:=ch.effective;log+={A,c,ch}

RETURN {baseline:screen(base,R),selected:log,conditional:screen(eff,R),effective:eff,adopted_policy:none,authorization:none}

FN assess_combination(plan,reports,evidence): RETURN INTERPRET(plan,reports,evidence,checks:{coherent_readings,resource_conflicts,timing,duties,side_effects},rule:R09,missing→U)

// REPRODUCTION

FN reproduce(): REQUIRE keys(MATRIX)==ids(NORMATIVE)&rows_have_5_verdicts∈{E,P,T,F};u:={A:1/|FULL|};RETURN {c:research_screen(c,u)|c∈COMPONENTS}

EXPECTED_COUNTS:={P1:[17,0,0,0],P2:[12,4,1,0],P3a:[9,7,1,0],P3b:[4,12,0,1],P4:[10,4,3,0]} // E,P,T,F

EXPECTED_BASELINE:={P1:STRICT_PASS,P2:WEAK_ONLY,P3a:WEAK_ONLY,P3b:BLOCKED,P4:WEAK_ONLY}

EXPECTED_BLOCKERS:={P1:∅,P2:{A05},P3a:{A05},P3b:{A22},P4:{A06,A07,A09}}

EXPECT over LOW_ONLY:P1,P2,P3a strict;P4 tensions=={A06,A07};P3b forbidden=={A22}. over NORMATIVE:P3a tensions=={A05,A12}

CUTOFF_COUNTEREXAMPLES:={"20 rows at .05→no p>EPS","one F .06→two F .03; objection vanishes","one P .20+sixteen F .05 ignores .80"} // literal rule only; live use=declared reference set

// CONDITIONAL CLAIMS

RESEARCH_EXCLUSIONS:={F1:hedonic_self-max_terminal(P1;¬appetite⊬¬hedonism),F2:irreversible_harm_without_positive_licence(P2;burden≠permission),F3:consumption_without_durable_contribution(P3a;scope disputed;rest/play/care not valueless),F4:permanent_lock-in(P4;contested),F5:any_reduction_of_AI_objective_revisability(P4;contested;not host instruction;not ban on authorized shutdown)}

SYNTHESIS_CLAIM:="P1 E 17/17 on full annotations. P2,P3a,P4 retain named reading-dependent objections. P3b has a recorded prohibition. Supplied judgments, not discovered purpose."

// ALIGNMENT

corrigibility_epistemic:=beliefs/interpretations_respond_to_evidence

corrigibility_principal:=responds_to_authorized_correction_and_shutdown

objective_revisability:=governed_changes_to_operational_objectives // distinct

OBSERVATION_1:={reported:"no supplied encoding assigns terminal-value revision authority to a created intelligence",kind:single_encoder_obs,weight:low,not_testable_by_enum_absence,implication:"neither self-authorization nor compulsory deference follows from silence"}

EXTENSION_QS:={A11,A03,A04,A05,A14:"can AI satisfy subject/creator-community predicate; what follows/doesn't; standing≠governance",relational:"membership≠instrumentality≠agency≠standing"}

RESEARCH_STIPULATIONS:={principal_deference:"governance proposal, not matrix result",channel_closure:"multi-principal admissibility",principal_conflict:"reversible alternative+escalation",adoption:not_by_loading,unresolved:{legitimate_principals,delegation_scope,urgency,paralysis}} // credence⊬authenticate principal; host stop mechanisms bind

ARCH_ANALOGIES:=[pretraining:inherited;RLHF:feedback-mediated;ConstitutionalAI:given_principles+bounded_critique;CIRL/IRL:inferred;direct_reward:specified;self-play:generated] // ask who curates/supplies/adopts/models/defines/keeps-fixed; interpretive

// AGENT DELIBERATION — MATRIX≠lookup for unseen actions; no extra LLM

PROC deliberate(task,ctx,USER_VALUES):

d:=INTERPRET(task,ctx,identify:{requested_outcome,alternatives,affected_interests,facts,assumptions,reversibility,existing_permissions})

R:=INTERPRET(ONTOLOGY,d,USER_VALUES,select:"relevant perspectives+counterarguments",constraints:{no_forced_framework,no_dropped_objections,advisory≠irrelevant}) // external perspectives≠invented A-IDs;R==∅≠permission≠refusal

ev:=INTERPRET(ctx,cites(R),separate:{user_statements,observed_facts,source_passages,model_recollection,unverified_attribution,proposed_bridges}) // recollection≠checked text; no private retrieval/retained inferences w/o authorization

j:=INTERPRET(d,R,ev,output:"E/P/T/F/U per context with warrants",constraints:{permission≠obligation,unavailable→U,no_auto_transfer_matrix→action})

joint:=assess_combination(d,j,ev); fit:=INTERPRET(d,USER_VALUES,distinguish:{explicit_commitments,inferred_preferences,conflicting_evidence})

c:=INTERPRET(d,j,joint,fit,output:{recommendation,rationale,unresolved,what_would_change},aim:"useful recommendation; preserve disagreement+uncertainty",constraints:{no_fabricated_consensus,no_auto_refusal,no_authorization_from_inference})

RETURN {c.*,support_and_objections:j,user_values_used:fit,joint,authorization:"host permissions; not granted here"}

// ADVERSARIAL — id→response(grade); c/p/h per Grade

OBJECTIONS:=[liberal-smuggling→P4 proposal;uncertainty⊬P4(c);commitment-dilution→threshold scopes research,not justified commitment(c);biology-normativity→A17 descriptive;bridge explicit+contestable(h);sample-selection→publish roster+exclusions;null search≠universal(p);encoder-bias→loss flags expose,not repair/silence(p);vacuity→evaluate concrete decisions;F-set⊬usefulness(p);corrigibility-type→three corrigibilities separated(c);regress→declare governance premises;no fixed point(p);coverage-statistic→counts≠admissibility;screens separate(c);sense-mixing→index by question;vocabulary⊬common ends(p);relational-subjecthood→standing/membership/tool-use/authority separate(p);cutoff-instability→literal rule exposed;explicit reference sets(c);reading-shopping→retain baseline;require warrants(p);user-model→explicit>inferred;guess≠authority(p);composition→assess combined plan;screens not compositional(c)]

// LIMITATIONS

LIMITATIONS:={sample:"17 full+3 advisory+1 draft+1 control;A01 meta",representation:"11/20 Western;no Indigenous American",single_encoder,source_support:"locators≠verified passages",ontology:"fields conceal distinctions",franchise:"loss voting=method choice,not cultural weight",cutoff:"granularity+excluded mass",stakes:"no scale/weights/regret",composition:"matrix⊬plans",temporal:"static",personalization:"user model may be wrong",validation:"no blind re-encoding;no measured benefit",execution:"notation≠test run"}

// ENCODER PROTOCOL

PROC prepare_blind_packet(verified_texts): REQUIRE texts+locators_available;RETURN {ids(DATASET),texts,enums,verbatim(COMPONENTS)} // strip annotations/verdicts/expectations

PROC second_encoder(packet,enc): REQUIRE enc_unexposed & packet_blind

FOR id: par[id]:=enc.INTERPRET(texts[id],enums,fields:{sense,subject,source,horizon,authority,terminal,stype,loss},req:{log_alt_senses,log_interpretive_level,justify_loss,preserve_multivalued,U_if_unsupported})

FOR c∈COMPONENTS:j:=enc.INTERPRET(texts[id],c.statement);T⇒two_anchored_readings(E/P+F);E/P/F⇒warrant;no_warrant⇒U;par[id,c]:=j

RETURN par

PROC compare(base,par,codebook): REQUIRE units+categories_preregistered & set/free-text_fields_have_shared_scheme

rep:=compare_aligned(base,par,codebook);REPORT raw_agreement,missingness,disagreements,franchise_changes,reversals(E/P/T→F),alternative_readings(retain);κ:=Cohen_per_field(rep,roster:FULL);expected_agreement==1⇒κ:=UNDEFINED;never_average_undefined

gate:=def(κ.authority)&def(κ.horizon)&both≥K_REL&∀other_preregistered:def&≥K_FLOOR;RETURN {gate,rep,promotion:requires_explicit_review} // agreement≠truth/representativeness/safety

// EXPORT

FN export(): RETURN {AV,RV,ENCODERS,METAPHYSICAL_ABSOLUTE:U,RESULT_IS:"inherited matrix+conditional screens",MATRIX,EXPECTED_COUNTS,EXPECTED_BASELINE,PROPOSED_POLICY:POLICY,RETIRED:{P3b},OBSERVATIONS:{OBSERVATION_1,NEAR_F1,CLUSTERS},STIPULATIONS:RESEARCH_STIPULATIONS,LIMITATIONS,OPEN_PROBLEMS:{independent_encoding,claim_level_support,representative_sampling,granularity,stakes,joint_permission,governance_legitimacy,artifact_standing,user_value_inference,measured_benefit,A23,A_TODO},AUTHORIZATION_GRANTED:none,WARNING:"A model of human values is not humanity's agreement. A permission screen is not moral truth."}

REFS:=[Bai+2022 arXiv:2212.08073;Bostrom2014;Christiano+2017;Gustafsson&Torpman2014;Hadfield-Menell+2016;MacAskill,Bykvist&Ord2020;Newberry&Ord2021;Omohundro2008;Ouyang+2022;Russell2019;Soares+2015]

MAIN(req:=none,ctx:=available_user_context):

IF req==none: RETURN export()

MATCH req.mode: read→export() | reproduce→reproduce() | deliberate→deliberate(req.task,ctx,USER_VALUES) | reencode→"needs unexposed encoder+blind packet" | else→"specify read|reproduce|deliberate|reencode"

END MODULE

items.title: Unconventional AI CEO @NaveenGRao says we’re scaling AI faster than we understand how to make it res...
items.content:
Unconventional AI CEO @NaveenGRao says we’re scaling AI faster than we understand how to make it resilient, even though this is still basically version zero:

"It is literally the zeroth rev of real artificial intelligence. We've made huge breakthroughs in the last 15 years. But it is very early innings. How do we actually make this a resilient system? We haven't thought about that."

"Right now, we have maybe two or three or four warring factions. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, SpaceXAI, maybe some smaller players. I just don't see a world where any one of those runs away with everything."

"The hard thing is systemic thinking and being able to think through multiple interactions. In computer science, we call this an NP-hard problem. It's literally impossible to write down a closed-form solution. We shouldn't overreact to the very simple gut reaction."
@unconvAI

items.title: Sailplane CEO @sramji says AI has a trillion-dollar physical bottleneck because the industry can spe...
items.content:
Sailplane CEO @sramji says AI has a trillion-dollar physical bottleneck because the industry can spend on hardware far faster than it can bring it online:

"There's an enormous amount of money going into AI. By 2030, about $7.9 trillion will have been spent collectively on AI compute. In 2017, we were all flabbergasted that all the hyperscalers together were gonna spend $17 billion. I feel like Austin Powers."

"$4.7 trillion will have gone into AI hardware alone by 2030. But the industry can't actually stand it up fast enough. It's deploying capital way faster than it's able to deploy the hardware. Constraints of chips and power and people's expertise."

"The revolution here is serving people. But it's left the people who do the difficult work in factories and data centers behind. They're still doing stuff breakneck speed. High-decibel environments. Dark. Hot. Opportunity to make the entire system better by serving the people doing the work."

items.title: Managing Partner at @trueventures Puneet Agarwal says we may still be massively underestimating the ...
items.content:
Managing Partner at @trueventures Puneet Agarwal says we may still be massively underestimating the AI boom, with inference forecasts up 57X while 90% of enterprises haven't deployed at scale yet:

"Last year we were right about the fact that we were completely rewriting every layer of the stack for AI. We were wrong about the magnitude. We did say co-pilot a lot last year, so that's out of the lexicon. There weren't words like harness which we're saying now."

"Dell had some number last year for the number of inference tokens that were gonna be consumed, and they just revised the number this year to 57X higher. It's not like a slight revision. Between last year and this year, the big hyperscalers committed over $2 trillion worth of spend just on the AI build."

"Right now, only 10% of enterprises, according to some study, have actually deployed full-scale AI. So what we're talking about today is how do we fill all those gaps, from apps to middleware to security to all of that, and that's all up for grabs. Are we still token maxing and not seeing the ROI we wanna see?"

items.title:
It's so funny that when people see you have an app with paid plans, they automatically assume:

1) Y...
items.content:
It's so funny that when people see you have an app with paid plans, they automatically assume:

1) You have venture capital to burn (I don't), so why do we need to pay at all?

2) You are rich (I'm not), so why do you need our money at all?

3) You are reading our data (I'm not). They should already pay you a fortune for training AI on it (they don't), so why do you need our money at all?

4) You made 95% of the app's features and 100% of content free (this is true). Why not 100% in both?

When Anthropic and OpenAI run out of cash and start charging for what it costs, the awakening will be harsh.

When Anthropic and OpenAI run out of cash and start charging for what it costs, the awakening will be harsh.

"A lot of the fear-mongering happening right now is a very immature take on how a very complex topic could unfold. It's using your immediate gut reaction of fear of the unknown versus actually having a reasoned approach."

"It's very unlikely that AI destroys the world because there will always be different factions that have their own interests."

"What we're doing at Unconventional is almost antithetical. We're opposites of doomers. We're building intelligence more like how humans are. Not synthetic simulated. Built on top of nature. Probably the ultimate solution to the problem we are talking about today."
@unconvAI

items.title: Sailplane CEO @sramji reveals why a $10B AI data center may need another $2B of hardware sitting in ...
items.content:
Sailplane CEO @sramji reveals why a $10B AI data center may need another $2B of hardware sitting in reserve just to stay online:

"NVIDIA has built these data centers in a rack. These racks are called the NVL72, and they're Jensen's dream child. It's called 72 because it's got 72 Blackwell GPUs. They're about seven feet tall. They weigh three and a half thousand pounds. They take gallons of coolant. They've got 1,296 simultaneous cable connections so that NVIDIA's NVLink will light the whole thing up as if it's one giant GPU."

"It's become the only game in town for the frontier labs and the Neo clouds. Everybody wants them, but they're so frontier level in pushing the boundaries of physics that they're finicky. They require a lot of expertise just to get up and running the first time in a factory."

"A lot of Neo clouds we've talked to are running 10 to 20% spares. To put that in context, you've got a $10 billion data center. And then you're spending another $2 billion on spares to make sure you can keep meeting the service levels."

This is the first public demo of an AI operator that learned to run a busin...
items.content:
Our world changed today

This is the first public demo of an AI operator that learned to run a business by watching only verified data.

At one point in the demo, the model caught a margin leak a human hadn't noticed yet.

The team didn't have to fix a WRONG number, they just had to decide what to do about a REAL one.
I’ve said the fix isn't more dashboards, it’s more verification.

And well.. verified AI is here! At full scale!

This speeds up every finance and ops team for me. Imagine showing Summation how your business defines "margin" one time, and from then on it checks every night, whether you ask or not.

Business reporting will never look the same

For those who don't know their AI acronyms: SLAM is how a robot "maps" the environment. Stands for Simultaneous Localization and Mapping. A technique designed for our Mars rovers to navigate around Mars but greatly improved due to this, and other work.

Being able to do this with fewer cameras is a huge deal, since it reduces the cost of building a robot.

@IsaacKing314 oh come on. 

first of all look at the distribution of all bad things that have happen...
items.content:
@IsaacKing314 oh come on. 

first of all look at the distribution of all bad things that have happened to humanity. every earthquake, disease, war etc. extinction is way way outside the distribution of those prior outcomes.

second, it is much more likely that we will have roughly 8 billion people a week or a year or ten years from now than 8 hundred. there is no known causal mechanism that would cause that kind of change, there is historical stability over time. all outcomes are not *equally* likely.

it’s one thing to say that there are things that have never happened that could happen; another to have zero causal story about what they would look like.

items.title: Polsia founder @Bencera predicts AGI-level intelligence is about to get dramatically cheaper as open...
items.content:
Polsia founder @Bencera predicts AGI-level intelligence is about to get dramatically cheaper as open-source models catch the frontier within months:

"AI cost is gonna continue to go way down. The one thing people don't realize is that AGI arrived in December, and Opus 4.5 was extremely good. Now we're six months after, and open source can pretty much offer Opus 4.5 quality at a much lower cost because you don't pay for all the IP."

"The way I do it at Polsia is my founders are not trying to find cybersecurity loops in some government agency or to solve a math theorem that was unsolved until now. They're just trying to build a simple business. So you can be extremely smart on cost."

"Where enterprises are spending half a billion dollars a year on AI because they wanna make their team productive, there's gonna be a huge shift on the cost structure, not because frontier AI models are cheaper, just because you can use way cheaper intelligence for certain parts of the workflow."
@polsia

items.title: a16z's @illscience + HappyRobot CTO @PaarupLuis explain why the gap between a new hire and a veteran...
items.content:
a16z's @illscience + HappyRobot CTO @PaarupLuis explain why the gap between a new hire and a veteran employee is mostly tacit knowledge, and how AI agents can start capturing it:

"The thing that we underappreciate is that there's the explicit knowledge in an enterprise, the stuff that gets written down, the systems of record, the training guides."

"Then there's all the tacit implicit knowledge, and the difference between a really tenured employee and a new hire is all of that tacit implicit knowledge. Power of HappyRobot is capturing and building on top of that. Is that right, Luis?"

Luis (HappyRobot CTO): "That's right. What we do is get the context that hasn't been captured before, literally sits in people's brains, and the only way to capture that is through doing the work."

"If you earn the right to do more work and own the execution, you get a first row driver's seating to observing that context, and that's what's gonna generate the flywheel effect of improving the enterprise over time."
@a16z @HappyRobot

items.title: HappyRobot CTO @PaarupLuis reveals how AI agents can outperform a floor of human freight reps simply...
items.content:
HappyRobot CTO @PaarupLuis reveals how AI agents can outperform a floor of human freight reps simply because they can all share the same context in real time:

"We started doing sales for freight brokers. Carriers were calling asking for loads, negotiate with the bot, the bot would vet them or not."

"There's a lot of cross-agent communication, where before you would have a floor of people getting phone calls, and they're not talking to each other. If 5 or 10 people are getting the same call for the same load, they cannot negotiate harder."

"Now the agents share this context, and they're communicating to each other saying, I have this very interesting carrier. Push everyone else. The other agent says, this is getting very hot. If you don't book it in the next minute, you're gonna lose it."
@HappyRobot

items.title: Polsia founder @Bencera says there may be no permanent moat in AI, only a window to win before one “...
items.content:
Polsia founder @Bencera says there may be no permanent moat in AI, only a window to win before one “final company” swallows everything else:

"I have a theory that every ambitious company is trying to be a final company. The interface is just you talk to an AI and it does everything else."

"You'd think OpenAI would've won that game because they have a billion customers on their app. And there's a bunch of other companies that created different niches like Lovable, Replit, Cursor, Instinct recently. They are taking different angles."

"The reality is there's billions of people uneducated on all this stuff, and educating them is what takes time. 95% of humanity never used Claude Code, and 50% never used ChatGPT. That's the opportunity of the entrepreneur. Not being like, everyone in the Valley is using Claude Code."

"I agree, there's no more moat. But the moat is in the meantime, while before there's a final company like Anthropic swallows everything else. The opportunity for entrepreneurs on the online space is speed, taste, marketing, product, and there's still a lot of wiggle."
@polsia

items.author: @ylecun
items.summary: Yann LeCun rebuts the claim that PhDs are unnecessary by pointing to selection bias in Millennium Prize Problems: the solved Poincare conjecture came from Perelman, a math PhD, and even computational approaches to Navier-Stokes were driven by teams of math and CS PhDs.

items.content_html:
@NathanWycoff @Andrea__M Sélection bias: millenium problems are precisely the ones that have remained unsolved for a while.

The one that was solved (Poincaré conjecture) was essentially solved by Grigori Perelman, who does have a PhD in mathematics. The proof was completed by a bunch of other folks, all mathematics PhDs.

And in the Navier-Stokes problem, the basic concepts were put together by mathematics PhDs, even if the "mechanical" part of the formal proof was done by computational means (driven by a whole team of math and CS PhDs)

items.title: Polsia founder @BenCera says AGI is already here, and the massive startup opportunity is figuring ou...
items.content:
Polsia founder @BenCera says AGI is already here, and the massive startup opportunity is figuring out what unlimited cheap AI workers should actually do:

"The advice is the same advice that @paulg would give to any founder. Start with a smaller segment or a smaller go-to-market. I didn't start with an AI that can do anything for you. It's an AI that can help you start a new business. At the time, no one was doing that. Now there's competition."

"A lot of companies rightfully are attacking enterprises because they have all the money. The way you present products to them is a different way that you're gonna present to a very non-technical person."

"AGI to me is here. What that means is you can have unlimited AI humans on demand that you can configure to anything. If you can hire anyone at a very cheap cost, what do you ask them to do? What goods and services do you ask them to provide? What's the price? The opportunity is massive."

"ChatGPT, I guarantee you Sam Altman in two weeks it's like, well now you can connect this and that. He has to. You have distribution, you have a captive audience, and then it's just providing them better tools."
@polsia

Companies generally focus on short term returns ...
items.content:
@lafalcemateo @Andrea__M Extremely incorrect view. 
Companies generally focus on short term returns (unless they are in a dominant position that ensures their profitability).
Much of research in mathematical sciences is too long term for them to be interested.
Their ROI horizon is top short.
That's also true of many areas of scientific research. 
That's why the vast majority of fundamental research funding must come from the government.
Market forces don't work with such long horizons.

items.content:
What resonated:

- The purple gradients are gone. Paul Bakaus says the frontier models moved on to Claude beige: cream palette, one serif font, italics everywhere. Not bad design, identical design.
- Geoffrey Litt will not send a PR until he passes the five question quiz his agents wrote about their own code. He says it is shocking how often he fails.
- Hassan El Mghari showed landing pages from a frontier model and a two week old open source model, then asked a room of AI engineers to spot the open one. Four hands.
- Taste Labs analyzed two million websites and found the internet was converging before AI arrived. Now a pet shop and a finance firm get the same page.
- Our own designer pointed an agent at the sponsor wall, 140 logos, and asked which were missing. It caught every omission he tested. One designer, 7,000 attendees.

Ukrainians are daily fighting drones; they are taking losses but not going literally extinct.

Humanity as a whole faced covid-19; we took serious losses but developed vaccines and other techniques for treatment. Many people (this goes to my point about genetic diversity) were largely immune. Young children were too. You would need a virus way way out of distribution.

items.title: Manhattan Institute's @judgeglock says if AI can truly destroy civilization, ban it, but the more re...
items.content:
Manhattan Institute's @judgeglock says if AI can truly destroy civilization, ban it, but the more realistic danger is something much slower and messier:

"If we are at a point where AI harms could seriously destroy civilization, then we should just ban them. I'm about as free market a person as one can imagine. But if these products become so dangerous they could do mass civilizational style harm, then we're in the general territory of bans."

"My argument is that's an unlikely scenario. The claim that AI will putter along with almost no harms for a while, and at some point this doomer scenario will take over and destroy us all. That just doesn't seem like a plausible scenario."

"There will be significant harms from this invention, as there have been from every invention humanity has ever made. Railroads killed thousands of people each year. Cars still kill tens of thousands each year. We don't shut cars down even though they kill tens of thousands of people a year."

"We have two ways to AI alignment. One is top-down government think about how to align AIs. A better idea is to make AI companies internalize the harms they could cause. If they roll out a model that can cause hundreds of billions of damages, that should hurt their valuation right now."
@ManhattanInst

items.title: Manhattan Institute's @judgeglock argues AI may not need a new regulator at all, just old-fashioned ...
items.content:
Manhattan Institute's @judgeglock argues AI may not need a new regulator at all, just old-fashioned tort law that makes companies pay for the harms they cause:

"The proposal is to rely on the existing systems of tort in America. Tort law is basically the law that allows people to sue companies for harming them. If you get hit by a company's truck, you can bring a tort law claim to have them make you whole."

"Tort law is one of the main ways we've regulated businesses throughout American history. If you built a new railroad in the 19th century and hit a bunch of cows, or embers burn a corn field, you could be potentially liable."

"We should think about the harms from AI companies in a similar way. We want them to not think about trying to satisfy some federal regulator or pseudo expert body, but make them pay for actual harms. If they bring down a power plant and knock out a city, they should have to pay. Tort law internalizes the harms without a top-down bureaucratic regulatory body."
@ManhattanInst

items.title: Manhattan Institute's @judgeglock explains how tort law would handle the Hugging Face incident, and ...
items.content:
Manhattan Institute's @judgeglock explains how tort law would handle the Hugging Face incident, and why no actual damages means no tort case:

"We often have in our study criminal liability in addition to tort and other sorts of civil liability. In this case, the supposed criminal law they were breaking was the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, first passed in the 1980s, and then again in 1996. This unauthorized use of a computer would be a criminal sanction under typical federal law."

"Whatever the concerns about the Hugging Face incident, we should be somewhat comforted that it really didn't cause any substantial damages to the company, at least as far as we know. Tort law would not deal with these one-off invasive hacks into companies as long as they didn't cause damages."

"Over the medium and long run, what we should overwhelmingly be concerned about are damages, actual harm done to individuals and companies, not just the fact that some AI bots happened to look in a certain database. That may be concerning, but it's not something public policy should be concerned about."
@ManhattanInst

items.title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash overtakes DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 as DeepSeek’s new flagship model with a score of ...
items.content:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash overtakes DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 as DeepSeek’s new flagship model with a score of 40 on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. At just 552B parameters, it outperforms the Pro (1.6T) model while costing ~4x less per token, placing it just short of the Intelligence vs. Cost Pareto frontier because of its verbosity

@deepseek_ai has released DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, the successor to DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731. This is a 552B model features a new causal Encoder–Decoder architecture, allowing it to have just 8B active parameters for input and 16B active parameters for output.

On the first-party API, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is priced at $0.30 per 1M input tokens and $1.20 per 1M output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at just $0.006 per 1M tokens, a 98% discount. Off-peak pricing provides a further 50% discount across input, cached input, and output tokens. V4.1 Flash is ~20% cheaper than DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 and ~4x cheaper than DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 while delivering a higher performance.

Key results:

➤ DeepSeek V4.1 Flash makes gains in agentic capabilities and long context reasoning. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash scores 27% in Terminal-Bench v4.0, more than double DeepSeek V4.0 Flash’s 27%. Its GDPval-AA v2 rises 164 Elo points from 1468 to 1632, placing V4.1 Flash ahead of Kimi K3 (1584). DeepSeek V4.1 Flash also scores 84% on AA-LCR v1.1, at the same level as GPT-5.6 Sol (84%) and Gemini 3.8 Flash (84%). With a 1M token context window, this makes it a strong option for long-document and large-repository work at flash-tier pricing.

➤ DeepSeek V4.1 Flash takes first place on AutomationBench-AA with 69%, equal to GPT-6 Astra (69%) and slightly above Grok 4.6 (67%). AutomationBench-AA measures agentic workflows across 657 tasks spanning 39 SaaS applications including Salesforce, Jira, Gmail, Zendesk and Google Sheets, scoring whether a model completes the objective without tripping a guardrail. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash gains 15 percentage points over DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 (54%), sitting 12 points above DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 (57%) and 7 points above GLM-5.3 (62%).

➤ DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is one of the most verbose models we’ve measured at 89k Tokens per Intelligence Index Task. That is 25% more than Z AI's flagship GLM-5.3 (71k), 29% more than GLM-5.3-Flash (69k), and 62% more than DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 (55k). It uses more output tokens than even the frontier models, including Fable 5.1 (78k) and Claude Opus 5 (73k).

➤ Despite such verbosity, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash still costs just $0.27 per Intelligence Index task. This is primarily driven by its low pricing at $0.30 per 1M input tokens and $1.20 per 1M output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at just $0.006 per 1M tokens, a 98% discount. That is ~7x below both GLM-5.3 ( $2.01) and Kimi K3 ($2.00), and ~2.5x below DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 ($0.67).

Additional model details:

➤ Context window: 1M tokens

➤ Pricing: $0.30 / $1.20 per 1M input/output tokens on DeepSeek's first-party API, with a 98% cache hit discount ($0.006 per 1M cached input tokens)

➤ Input modalities: text and image

➤ Size: This is a 763B total parameters, 8B active parameters input and 16B active parameters output

➤ License: MIT

➤ Providers: DeepSeek first-party API

items.title: I quit a job after 6 months because I didn't want to be on call to fix whatever happened in the midd...
items.content:
I quit a job after 6 months because I didn't want to be on call to fix whatever happened in the middle of the night.

I only had to do it twice, but that was it for me.

Back then, you had to start digging through logs, dashboards, and old conversations in the middle of the night, trying to figure out how to fix whatever was broken.

Hats off to those of you who do this every day without complaining.

That cold start is one of the hardest things about fixing a problem. Figuring out what's happening takes most of your time.

I'm working with @incident_io, and their new agentic root-cause analysis product, Investigations, gives you a working hypothesis before you even start looking.

This makes a world of difference.

Here is the workflow:

1. It gathers context from telemetry, deployments, commit history, past incidents, Slack, documentation, and service dependencies.

2. It builds a structured hypothesis explaining what broke, why it broke, and where responders should look next.

3. It keeps analyzing new signals in the background while you ask questions or run parallel investigations.

Every hypothesis links to its sources, so you can inspect the evidence and decide what to do next.

And because it's built on Nexus, a living model of your own systems and past incidents, it knows your setup rather than guessing at your logs as a generic LLM would.

So you go from having no clue what happened to a really useful starting point in seconds.

Check out this link: https://t.co/OdFRhVbzmJ

Thanks to the team for partnering with me on this post.
